nameStory: The triangle barnacle gets its name from its distinctive three-sided, triangular shape when viewed from above. This geometric form sets it apart from the more rounded or oval shapes of most other barnacle species, making it relatively easy to spot once you know what to look for.
description: Triangle barnacles are small, cone-shaped marine creatures that cement themselves permanently to rocks, shells, and human-made structures underwater. These invasive animals have six shell plates that form steep-sided walls around their soft bodies, colored in distinctive dark pink hues. Originally from the Pacific Ocean, they've hitchhiked around the world on ship hulls and now call New England waters home too.

idTips.label: Triangular shape
idTips.description: The shell forms a distinct three-sided pyramid when viewed from above, rather than the circular or oval shape of most barnacles

idTips.label: Dark pink color
idTips.description: The shell plates have a characteristic dark pink or reddish-pink coloration that stands out against lighter-colored surfaces

idTips.label: Six shell plates
idTips.description: The cone is made up of six separate, interlocking plates that fit together like puzzle pieces, visible as distinct seam lines

idTips.label: Steep-sided walls
idTips.description: The sides rise sharply from the base, creating a tall, pointed cone rather than a low, rounded dome

idTips.label: Hard, calcified texture
idTips.description: The shell feels rock-hard and gritty to the touch, with a rough, chalky surface that won't give under pressure

habitat: Triangle barnacles attach to hard surfaces in subtidal zones - the areas that remain underwater even at low tide. Look for them on rocky shores, pier pilings, dock infrastructure, and ship hulls in harbors and protected coastal waters. They prefer areas with good water circulation but not heavy wave action.

seasonality.spring: Adults are actively filter-feeding as water temperatures rise, extending their feathery feeding appendages from their shells when underwater.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with visible feeding behavior and potential reproduction, though the animals themselves look the same year-round.
seasonality.fall: Continued activity as adults prepare for winter, with steady filter-feeding when submerged.
seasonality.winter: Less active but still alive, remaining tightly closed most of the time in cold water temperatures.

funFact: This species was first scientifically described by none other than Charles Darwin himself, who was fascinated by barnacles and spent eight years studying them before publishing his theory of evolution!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other rock barnacles, but the triangle barnacle's three-sided shape is unique - if you can trace three distinct sides forming a triangle from above, you've found your species. Memory trick: 'Triangle barnacle, triangular top!'
contextualKnowledge: As an invasive species in New England waters, triangle barnacles compete with native barnacles and other marine life for space on hard surfaces. They're considered 'fouling organisms' because they grow on ship hulls and dock infrastructure, requiring regular cleaning and maintenance.
compareHints: Unlike its relatives the wrinkled barnacle and rough barnacle, which are more circular or oval-shaped, the triangle barnacle has that distinctive three-sided form. The wrinkled barnacle has prominent ridged patterns, while the rough barnacle has a more irregular, bumpy surface - but neither has the geometric triangular outline of this species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wrinkled barnacles are much smaller and more delicately built than their cousin the rough barnacle, with distinctly ridged shells that feel gritty to touch.
Rough barnacles are larger and much more coarsely textured than wrinkled barnacles, which have smoother shells with fine ridges.
